newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military to study possible Zaire evacuation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military to study possible Zaire evacuation.

text.p: A team of U.S. military specialists is on route to Zaire to study airfields, roads and communications in case a decision is made to evacuate Americans, the Pentagon said on Wednesday.

Army Lt. Col. Nancy Burt, a Pentagon spokeswoman, said the team of about 30 was to arrive in neighbouring Congo and Gabon later in the day but stressed the visit did not signal any decision to evacuate Americans from civil war-torn Zaire.
"This does not represent any commitment or intention by the United States to deploy other forces into the region," she said. "Deployment of any forces would require a separate decision."

Burt said about 650 Americans, including U.S. government workers, were in the central African nation but no request had been made by the U.S. Embassy in the capital of Kinshasa to remove any of them to safety.

Members of the U.S. team were to arrive in Congo's capital of Brazzaville and Gabon's capital of Libreville from Europe and planned to move later into Zaire. "They will look at things like infrastructure, airfields, roads and communications," Burt said.
Other U.S. officials said the decision had been made because of advances by rebels seeking to topple the government of Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Any move to evacuate Americans by U.S. Marines and Air Force units would represent the latest in a series of post-Cold War missions for the U.S. military based in Europe and would come on the heels of last week's evacuation of hundreds of Americans from Albania.

The United States, meanwhile, said on Wednesday it continued to recognise Kengo wa Dondo as prime minister despite a vote in Zaire's transitional parliament to oust him. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said it was unclear whether Tuesday's parliamentary vote was constitutionally sound and it was up to the Zairean people to figure that out.
"Until they figure it out, it seems to us to be the best way forward to continue to recognise the Kengo government and to work with it," he said.
Kengo was in Kenya for talks on the crisis in Zaire. His presence ended a Zairean boycott of two previous rounds of Nairobi talks on the crisis.
Burns noted that leaders of other states in the region were participating and had issued an appeal for a ceasefire in the conflict. He said Washington joined in that appeal.

Mobutu, who has spent most of his time in Europe since cancer surgery there in August, had been in a hospital in Monaco. But Mobutu, apparently planning to return home this week to face the fast-spreading revolt, left the hospital on Wednesday. according to witnesses.
